title: The true devotee
hook: titles mean nothing without the life that matches

segments.voice: Yesterday, the true scholar: the pandit who teaches his own mind first. Your line was teach your own mind. Did you try your own advice? Today, ashtpadi nine turns to the devotee. Day four hundred seventy-two.

Someone volunteers at a shelter every Saturday, and makes sure to post a photo every time. Someone else drives an elderly neighbor to the doctor every month for years and never mentions it to anyone. Both did good. But if you had to guess which one was really devoted, you'd probably guess the second. Not because photos are wicked. Because the second one clearly wasn't waiting for anything back. Ashtpadi nine has two stanzas about devotees, and both of them land on exactly that point.
screen: `A PHOTO EVERY SATURDAY.` → `A NEIGHBOR DRIVEN FOR YEARS.` → `WHO WASN'T WAITING FOR ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: One stanza takes the title vaishnav, a devotee of Vishnu, a name honored across India. It says: the true vaishnav is the one with whom God is well pleased, who lives apart from the pull of maya, the passing world. Then the striking line: karam karat hovai nihkaram. Doing deeds, he remains without deeds. Nihkaram means free of the deed, free of its grip. It doesn't mean doing nothing. It means doing the good thing without hooking yourself to the result. The stanza says it plainly in the next lines: he doesn't hanker after the fruit of any action; he is absorbed only in devotion and the singing of praise. The next stanza takes another devotee's title, bhagauti, and says the same in a different key: the true one is dyed in love for God, leaves bad company behind, and every doubt dissolves from the mind. Two titles, one point. Devotion is measured by the life underneath it, and especially by whether it's waiting for a reward. The neighbor who drives someone to the doctor for years isn't keeping score. That's karam karat hovai nihkaram. The deed is done. The doer isn't clinging. This is not a criticism of the people who held these titles; the stanzas honor the names by asking them to be true. It's a mirror, held up to anyone who calls themselves devoted, in any community. Sikhs have a word for selfless service: seva. Its whole point is the same: the life, not the title.
screen: `VAISHNAV: AN HONORED NAME.` · `NIHKARAM: DOING, BUT NOT GRIPPED.` · `NO HANKERING FOR THE FRUIT.` · `BHAGAUTI: DYED IN LOVE.` · then, large: `THE LIFE, NOT THE TITLE.`

segments.voice: The practice: live one value quietly. Choose one value you care about: kindness, honesty, patience, generosity. Now picture one small act of it you could do today, where no one will see, and you won't mention it afterward. Wiping a shared table. Paying a compliment to someone's back. Leaving a good review for a stranger's small shop. Hold that picture. Notice any little wish to be noticed, and let it go on the out-breath. Breathe in: the deed. Breathe out: no reward. The bell holds the time.
The true devotee. Karam karat hovai nihkaram: doing deeds, yet free of them, hankering after no reward.
Your line: the life, not the title. Today, do your quiet good deed, and don't tell anyone, not even tonight. Day four hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara and beyond, and read these stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib as describing devotion that seeks no reward.

fork.setup: you've done a real good deed. nobody saw. what does the true devotee in ashtpadi nine do next?
options: post about it so it inspires others.
nothing: the deed is done, no reward sought.
fork.reveal: karam karat hovai nihkaram: the deed is done, and the doer isn't clinging to its fruit.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nihkaram, free of the deed; in ashtpadi nine, doing good without clinging to the result.

trapdoor: what you thought: a devotee is someone with a devout title.
what it means: the true devotee does good and hankers after no reward.
what a scholar hears: 'karam karat hovai nihkaram' echoes a wider Indic ideal of desireless action; ashtpadi nine places it inside the vaishnav stanza.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)

notes: Vaishnav stanza paraphrased: baisno so jis oopar suprasann / bisan kee maaiaa te hoe bhinn / karam karat hovai nihkaram / tis baisno kaa nirmal dharam / kaahoo fal kee ichhaa nahee baachhai / kevel bhagat keertan sang raachai. Confirm.
Bhagauti stanza paraphrased: bhagautee bhagvant bhagat kaa rang / sagal tiaagai dusat kaa sang / man te binsai sagalaa bharam. Confirm gloss of bhagauti.
Framing of vaishnav as an honored name, with no criticism of Vaishnava devotees; Keeper (and possibly a Hindu reviewer) should check.
Stanza order: the vaishnav and bhagauti stanzas appear to be pauris 2–3 and the pandit stanza (day 471) pauri 4, so the lessons teach them out of text order; confirm pauri numbers.
